newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS - Brazil seeks rating upgrade with Brady swap.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Brazil seeks rating upgrade with Brady swap.

text.p: Brazil is underpinning its bid for a debt rating upgrade and planting one more benchmark on its yield curve by offering to replace its Brady bonds with 30-year global bonds, the Central Bank said on Wednesday.

Gustavo Franco, the central bank's director of international affairs, said the swap would also reduce Brazil's external debt stockpile while improving its quality, taking some pressure off the Treasury's cash flow and cashing in some collateral.
"This operation will make the debt stock fall...and it reduces interest payments," Franco said. "The revenue from the operation will not be used to increase expenditure."
With the 30-year global issue, Brazil will have a sovereign benchmark at the long end of the yield curve, allowing it to take advantage of pent-up demand for high-yielding paper.
Franco said the issue would "price the Brazil risk at critical maturities," with room left in the 10 to 15 year range for future placements, such as a planned Italian lire Eurobond.
Perhaps most importantly, the operation is part of a long-running campaign to improve Brazil's risk rating.
Standard and Poor's Corp recently upgraded Brazil to BB minus from B plus. Still, both S&P and Moody's have hesitated to grant an investment-grade rating to Latin America's largest country.
"To have an investment grade, a country has to have a debt structure made up principally of traditional instruments, not restructured debt," Franco said.
Brazil is offering to swap par bonds BR4D24RR, discount bonds BRFLTD24RR and "C" bonds BR8D14RR for the 30-year global. The operation, launched Wednesday, will remain open until June 3,
It is also offering to buy back pars and discounts for cash and will accept cash offers on its global up to a value of 25 percent of the total issue.
There is no fixed upper limit to Brazil's buyback and swap offer, and theoretically it could involve the entire $26 billion stock of restructured Bradies held by Brazil.
It is the third such operation in emerging debt market. Mexico led the pack last April and the Philippines followed in September.
The Brazilian central bank last year battled for months with the Senate for permission to engage in swaps and buybacks.

Franco said the bank had waited since the Mexican operation for the right opportunity to make its offer. The decision Tuesday by the Federal Reserve not to raise U.S. interest rates opened "a good window," he said.
He said he was very satisfied with the reception given the swap in New York, where the liquid "C" bond settled 1-3/8 higher at 78-5/8 by late morning.
And he said he expected the operation to proceed calmly because of next week's Memorial Day holiday in the United States and a bank holiday in Brazil next Friday.

Franco also dismissed suggestions that a political scandal in Brazil could damp investor interest in the offer. Several deputies face accusations of accepting bribes to vote in favour of a measure to allow President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's re-election.
